definition: A professional preference for unevenly-distributed ("unbalanced") in-between spacing over a textbook-symmetric ease — concentrating detail heavily on one side of a motion (commonly the arrival) while leaving the rest sparse or linear — stated as reading better than an evenly-balanced ease in and ease out.
purpose: Make a motion feel more dynamic and less "textbook" by deliberately breaking left-right symmetry in how in-betweens are distributed, rather than defaulting to a matched ease-in/ease-out pair.
visible_effect: A motion that starts fast or loose (few or no in-betweens near the start) and only slows or eases heavily near one end, rather than an evenly-mirrored slow-fast-slow curve.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Professionally stated to read as more interesting and less flat than a symmetric ease — the named alternative pattern (all detail concentrated at the very end, everything else sparse or a single large jump) is called out as a common pattern experienced animators use, not a shortcut.
physical_interpretation: Real motion is rarely symmetric either — most physical accelerations and decelerations have different magnitudes and durations on each side, so an asymmetric spacing choice can be closer to how many real motions actually move than a matched, textbook-symmetric ease is.
use_cases: a motion wanting a confident, dynamic read rather than a soft, "balanced" ease
reducing authoring effort by collapsing most of a phase into few or no in-betweens while still landing cleanly, via detail concentrated only at the arrival
any professional-grade polish pass on an already-working, but visually flat, symmetric ease
non_use_cases: a motion where a matched, symmetric ease genuinely IS the correct physical or stylistic read (a pendulum, a smoothly decelerating object under even braking)
a first pass while still learning the basic mechanism — the video frames this as a refinement on top of understanding symmetric spacing first, not a replacement for learning it
interactions: Slow in/slow out — this is a refinement of that principle's own curve-shape choice, preferring an asymmetric curve over spacing_evenness's more neutral default

Pose hold density / mixed hold pacing — asymmetric spacing is most visible specifically when combined with varied hold density across a phase, per this video's own progression from "add in-betweens near the ends" to "remove nearly everything but the ends"
Exaggeration — an intentional imbalance is itself a selective-amplification choice (emphasize the arrival, restrain everywhere else), the same selectivity the existing `exaggeration` card asks for

style_variations.anime: the professional convention this entry is sourced from is explicitly Japanese TV animation production practice
style_variations.realistic: a matched, symmetric ease may read as more correct for genuinely symmetric real-world motion

cadence_representation: Partially reachable: `acceleration_contrast` and `spacing_evenness` already pick an easing style/DIRECTION on the keys bounding a phase (per the existing `slow_in_slow_out` card), which can already express an asymmetric ease-in-only or ease-out-only curve — what is not represented is this as a named PREFERENCE ("unbalanced often reads better") a caller could deliberately reach for, rather than an incidental possible value of an existing dimension.
control_surface: `acceleration_contrast` / `spacing_evenness` vocabulary dimensions, set asymmetrically (a different value or direction on each side of a phase) rather than matched.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion` already measures the actual velocity/acceleration curve per frame, which is sufficient to detect asymmetry directly (comparing the shape of the curve on either side of a phase's midpoint) — a real, buildable check from data this build already computes; nothing currently runs that specific comparison.
generation_or_modification_methods: `acceleration_contrast`/`spacing_evenness` already generate a curve; setting DIFFERENT values on the two bounding keys of one phase (rather than the same value mirrored) is how this build would already express asymmetry, if a caller chose to.
failure_modes: defaulting to symmetric spacing out of habit when an asymmetric read was actually wanted, producing the "flat," "boring," "too mechanical" result the video explicitly warns against
pushing asymmetry so far the motion reads as broken or unintentional rather than deliberately dynamic
roblox_considerations: None specific — a pure keyframe-spacing concept independent of the target engine.
examples: a ball's movement built up from a flat, evenly-spaced pass (called explicitly "flat," "boring," "too mechanical") to a version with extra in-betweens concentrated only near the two ends (video 8 @ 3:55–6:39)
a "common spacing chart pattern that pro animators use": removing nearly all the middle in-betweens and keeping only a single ease-in at the very end (video 8 @ 6:56–7:09)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/vSJ5lT_ma-E @ 3:55–7:09 — Dong Chang builds this progression live on screen with a visible spacing chart, describing a played-back result at each step; the specific played-back ball animation itself fell within a long static-screen stretch (3:29–9:19) that this session's sparse 27-frame sample for an 11-minute video did not capture distinctly, so this rests on the transcript's description rather than a directly-viewed play back; experimental until validated
